source.title: LINE: LLM-based Iterative Neuron Explanations for Vision Models
source.authors: Vladimir Zaigrajew; M. Piechota; Gaspar Sekula; Pawel Gelar; Przemysław Biecek

record.tranche_reason: The paper uses individual vision-model neurons as units for its explanation method and reports how well that method performs, but it does not test the stated neuron-pole job shares or the claim versions’ specific predictions.
record.gate_note: The CoSy results evaluate textual neuron-label quality, not the proportion of neurons with one or multiple jobs. The ablation experiments check whether removing a described visual concept changes activation; they do not measure the claimed job shares. The study does not test the language-model explanation claims in V6 or V7.
record.test_reason: The paper presents LINE, a neuron-labeling method for vision models (ResNet18/50, ViT-B/16, DINOv3), and reports how it performs against CLIP-Dissect, INVERT and DnD on CoSy AUC/MAD. It treats individual neurons as units to be labeled. It never measures the share of neurons with one or two jobs, never revisits InceptionV1 or pose, and never builds attribution graphs. CoSy scores how strongly a label's synthetic images activate the neuron relative to natural control images. It does not simulate activations on held-out text or natural data, so it does not bear on V6 or V7. Better tools giving higher label scores is related to V4, but no share of interpretable neurons is reported, so V4 is not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that LINE, a training-free black-box iterative labeler, achieves state-of-the-art CoSy performance, with AUC gains up to 0.11 on ImageNet and 0.05 on Places365. It discovers new concepts beyond predefined vocabularies (about 27% on average, up to 36%) and gives gradient-free visual explanations. They acknowledge that LINE may converge on one concept for polysemantic neurons, and that single labels risk an interpretability illusion.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies vision models, not language-model neuron poles. LINE iteratively proposes concepts and scores synthesized images; the paper does not conduct the original audit or measure one-job/two-job shares.
record.method_sensitivity: The selected top concept changes in 71% of cases when the T2I model is changed. The paper reports no significant activation-score difference between SDXL and FLUX.1[dev] (p = 0.7965), but reports SDXL significantly outperforming SD1.5 (p = 0.0375).

fits_no_version.finding: LINE gets higher CoSy AUC and MAD than CLIP-Dissect, INVERT and DnD in all six model/dataset settings in Table 1 (100 neurons each). Wilcoxon tests are significant except LINE vs CLIP-Dissect MAD on ResNet18 Places365 (p=0.1417). LINE-generated labels beat the predefined vocabulary for 16–36% of neurons (Table 2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: An iterative LLM plus text-to-image labeling loop gives vision-neuron labels with higher CoSy scores than single-pass vocabulary or captioning methods.

record.code_released: not stated (the text says the complete codebase is provided in supplementary material but gives no URL)
record.problems: The CoSy scores are aggregate results over 100 neurons and measure explanation-label performance rather than the prevalence of single-job neurons. The authors note that LINE can converge on a single concept for polysemantic neurons; the initial ImageNet vocabulary can bias discovery; and generative ablations can fail to remove the target or introduce reconstruction artifacts.
record.rows_left_out: No applicable claim-version results were omitted. The study's other reported analyses, including label-source proportions, optimization-step curves, visual-explanation comparisons, and T2I-model comparisons, do not measure the job shares or specific outcomes named in the claim versions.

untested.parts: Qwen3-32B neuron-pole shares (about 90% one job, 7% two related jobs, 2–4% not understood); no language model is studied.
Job shares across language models, dense and MoE, and across scale.
InceptionV1 cat/car neuron, pose as a shared feature, recursive generalization versus superposition.
The share of interpretable neurons and its rise with better tools or architectures; the paper reports only mean label scores, not a share of interpretable neurons, and does not study InceptionV1.
Attribution graphs from a model's own neurons and comparison with replacement models.
Whether explanations fitted to activating examples predict where the neuron fires on new inputs; CoSy uses synthetic concept images, not held-out activation prediction.
Simulation-based scoring of language-model neuron explanations.

record.verdict_notes: All 48 rows are the study's own method compared with baselines on an explanation-quality benchmark. All are correctly linked to 'none' and are not claim measures. The paper cites Bills et al. 2023 (an original source) only in passing. The high per-neuron AUCs (often ≥0.9) could look superficially consistent with 'neurons have one main job'. However, CoSy rewards the top concept's activation on synthetic images and does not measure monosemanticity or the share of interpretable neurons. The authors themselves warn that single labels compress polysemantic behaviour. The top concept changes in 71% of cases when the text-to-image model is swapped, which shows labels depend on the tool.

versions.untested_parts: Qwen3-32B neuron-pole shares and the reported proportions of one job, two related jobs, and not-yet-understood poles.
Neuron-pole job shares across language models, dense and mixture-of-experts architectures, and model scales.
The InceptionV1 cat-and-car example, pose as a shared feature, and recursive generalization versus superposition.
The proportion of interpretable neurons, its change with tools or architecture, and the estimates for InceptionV1-sized vision models.
Attribution graphs built from a large model’s own neurons and whether they explain behavior without a trained replacement model or its reconstruction error.
Whether explanations fitted to activating examples fail to predict where language-model neurons fire.
Automated scoring of language-model neuron explanations by simulating activations on new text.
